newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn to meet EMU aims, no Italy deal - Waigel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn to meet EMU aims, no Italy deal - Waigel.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Wednesday that Germany would qualify for European monetary union on time and denied reports that Bonn and Paris had hatched a deal to bar Spain and Italy from the starting lineup.
"Germany will fulfil the criteria of the Maastricht Treaty on time. That has been and remains our goal," Waigel told the German parliament's finance committee at a hearing on EMU.
The government's forecast of a rise in economic growth to 2.5 percent this year is realistic, and will help Germany meet the EMU targets, he said.

Asked about a report in the Italian business daily Il Sole 24 Ore that a deal was taking shape between France and Germany to keep Italy, and with it Spain, out of the first wave of countries hoping to join EMU, Waigel said, "There is none."

Waigel told the committee: "All countries that qualify will be able to participate in the first round. Others will be able to participate when they qualify, and no member will be arbitrarily excluded."
France also rejected the report about the plan to exclude Italy and Spain. "It's totally absurd," a French finance ministry official said.
And Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said there were no "secret deals" to keep Italy out of the start of Europe's planned single currency.
"I exclude that there are prejudicial attitudes against Italy and that there are secret accords," he told reporters.

Il Sole, quoting "sources in Bonn", said France had come round to the idea of keeping Italy and Spain out of the group of EMU founders because it feared Germany would otherwise insist on a two-year delay in the currency's planned January 1999 launch.
Germany was once considered a certainty for participation in EMU, and is still seen as an indispensible member of the team.
But it has lost ground on meeting the EMU deficit and debt targets, and must also contend with a deeply sceptical public.

Italy, once a long shot, has made breathtaking progress toward meeting the fiscal criteria, and has strong public backing. But many Germans are averse to Italy's entry, fearing it would soften the euro and make it prone to inflation.

Ciampi acknowledged on Wednesday there have been doubts about the sustainability of Italy's deficit-cutting measures of recent months. Italy's effort to slash its deficit-to-GDP ratio by four percentage points this year was "some undertaking".
"The doubts they have is to have a country in there with them whose continued behaviour is open to doubt," Ciampi said.

But he said it was important to have as many countries joining the euro as possible. "The strength of the (euro) is not so much a matter of how small it will be or how close to the deutschmark but how broad it will be," Ciampi said.
Doubts that Germany can meet the debt and deficit targets this year are raising questions about whether it will seek a delay in the planned January 1, 1999 start date or a softening of the criteria.
But Waigel insisted he has never wavered in his view that the Maastricht criteria should be strictly applied.
"Three-point-zero is three-point-zero", he said, hoping to dispel speculation that the deficit goal could be interpreted loosely.

Waigel said he could not exclude the possiblity that Germany's outstanding debt would exceed the Maastricht ceiling of 60 percent of gross domestic product this year, but that it would do what was needed to meet the targets.

The finance minister urged Germany's federal state governments to make explicit commitments to hold to the Maastricht guidelines, which are concerned with total public finances, not just at the federal level.
